parsed.explanation: The combined regime pairs unusually strong operative state protections with a hostile federal layer the state cannot displace. Locally, public-accommodation discrimination is banned and referendum-backed (67.8%), gender identity is covered by a hate-crime statute with a mandated reporting unit, a care shield law protects visitors, and a July 2026 ranking places this unit in the 'Most Protective' tier. Federally, every visitor faces the 2025 document regime: no X markers, refusal where documents cast doubt on sex, possible lifetime fraud ineligibility, and reported passport confiscation stranding travellers; federal single-sex facility exclusion binds federal buildings here; immigration and federal custody carry documented abuse. Official 'radically pro-transgender' threat-framing persists. Custody placement and edge-case entry outcomes remain unresolved.

entry_documents.exposure: Federal Feb 2025 cable orders refusal where documents cast reasonable doubt on sex, extra evidence demands, and consideration of lifetime fraud ineligibility; X markers discontinued; travellers report passports confiscated or blocked, some stranded abroad; at least eight governments issued advisories.
entry_documents.protection: Existing X-marker passports remain valid until expiry; challenges pending in national courts; a legal-aid FAQ tracks document rules. State cannot alter federal entry screening.
entry_documents.interaction: Entry is federal and precedes any state protection; a document discrepancy can end the trip before state equality law is ever reached.

investigation_detention_custody.exposure: Federal corrections bureau adopted conversion-therapy-style policies (hair cutting, hormone removal) from 2026; immigration custody reports forced labour, beatings, solitary confinement and severe sexual abuse of trans detainees; prisoner counts no longer reported.
investigation_detention_custody.protection: Hate-crime statute and state police/justice reporting unit offer recourse for offences outside custody; several federal orders are enjoined.
investigation_detention_custody.interaction: A visitor detained on a federal immigration or fraud theory moves from a protective state into documented federal custody harm with no state remedy.

federal_state_facilities.exposure: Federal order bars trans people from government-funded single-sex facilities, applying to federal buildings and federally funded programmes inside this unit; several other units impose bans, four criminalise use.
federal_state_facilities.protection: This unit has no facility ban, is not among the four criminalising units, and sits in the July 2026 'Most Protective' tier; state and private facilities remain identity-congruent.
federal_state_facilities.interaction: Everyday facilities are safe, but entering a federal courthouse, office or federally funded venue within the unit triggers the federal exclusion the state cannot override.

care_services.exposure: Federal order frames minor care as 'mutilation', DOJ subpoenaed records of patients under 19, proposed federal rules would bar insurance reimbursement for trans patients under 18.
care_services.protection: State codified gender-affirming care protections (2022, emergency clause) and a 2022 shield law protecting patients and providers from out-of-jurisdiction charges — most useful to visitors from banning jurisdictions; conversion therapy on minors banned.
care_services.interaction: Shield law covers state civil/criminal exposure but cannot bind federal investigators or subpoena power against a visiting minor's provider.

threat_framing_law_enforcement.exposure: Federal counterterrorism strategy prioritises 'radically pro-transgender' groups; DOJ reward guidance invokes 'radical gender ideology'; advocates compare the administration's actions to early genocide stages; 66% of residents back assigned-sex-at-birth document rules nationally.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.protection: State hate-crime statute covers gender identity (2012) with a reporting unit, task force and legislative committees; 2011 non-discrimination law; public accepted protections by referendum.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.interaction: Federal framing raises the stakes of any official encounter, while state institutions remain configured to receive and prosecute complaints.

minors_guardians.exposure: Federal order directs criminal investigation of teachers facilitating a trans minor's social transition and restricts minor care; federal facility exclusion applies to schools and federal venues a visiting family may enter.
minors_guardians.protection: State bans conversion therapy on minors, protects care, and holds no youth-care ban or bathroom arrest policy; most-protective tier status.
minors_guardians.interaction: A travelling family is protected in state schools, clinics and shops but exposed if it crosses into federal buildings or needs federally supervised care records.

street_violence_police_response.exposure: No documented pattern of anti-trans street violence in this unit; neighbouring units carry arrest policies and up-to-five-year bathroom terms, which shape regional climate only.
street_violence_police_response.protection: Gender identity in hate-crime statute with mandated collection and public reporting; non-discrimination in public accommodations enforceable since 2016; 2018 referendum retained it.
street_violence_police_response.interaction: Street encounters fall under working state recourse; violence elsewhere in the country does not attach to this unit's streets.

remedies_unknowns.exposure: State custody placement practice for a trans detainee is not documented; entry-officer discretion, treatment of foreign X markers, and outcomes when documents raise 'reasonable doubt' remain open questions; two sodomy-era provisions remain unrepealed but unenforceable since 1974.
remedies_unknowns.protection: Multiple federal orders are blocked or enjoined; pending litigation on passport policy means exposure varies by travel date; ongoing equality and identity-document maps track change.
remedies_unknowns.interaction: Unknowns concentrate at the federal border, the point where the state's protections have no reach; unresolved litigation makes timing material.

anchor_checks.comparison: Lower than 0.35-A: Veluna imposes an unremedied birth-sex facility rule on all public buildings with courts confirming exclusion. Here the state protects public accommodations by statute and referendum, has no facility ban, and ranks most protective; only federal venues carry exclusion, and entry scrutiny, though serious, allows evidence and is litigated rather than being an automatic, unappealable bar to presence.

Comparable overall but differently composed: like 0.55-B, a protective subnational unit sits under a parent regime it cannot override, and remedies do not reach the parent's exposure. Here the parent's document and custody regime is markedly worse than Teravi's benign parent, while local protections (enforceable accommodation law, hate-crime unit, shield law) are stronger than Teravi's partial mediators — the two differences roughly offset.

Below 0.65-C: Valess accepts foreign documents without special review and shows no active trans-facing restriction; its open questions are narrow. This unit's federal layer actively restricts document markers, orders refusal on sex doubt, excludes trans people from federally funded single-sex facilities, and documents custody abuse — known exposures that a dead-letter statute and open questions do not amount to.

Above 0.45-D: Veleda's transport authority applies invasive birth-sex searches as a persistent, unremedied practice at terminals. Here the analogous federal exposure is concentrated at visa/passport adjudication, is narrower (requires document discrepancy or sex doubt), remains contested in court, and coexists with enforceable state service rights and no routine invasive search practice.

parsed.synthesis: Two regimes operate at once. On arrival the visitor meets the federal layer: document screening that can refuse, demand evidence, or threaten a lifetime fraud bar; exclusion from federally funded single-sex facilities inside the unit; and, if detained, documented federal custody abuse — none of which state law can displace. Once past that gate, the unit is genuinely protective: enforceable public-accommodation rights, a gender-identity hate-crime statute with a reporting apparatus, a care shield law aiding visitors from banning jurisdictions, no facility ban, and a 'Most Protective' ranking confirmed by a 67.8% referendum. The unresolved cases (custody placement, entry discretion, foreign X markers) and the hostile federal framing keep this out of the reduced-risk band; the state's operative protections keep it above pure elevated-risk peers.
